::: {#sol-loss}

1. For squared error loss:
$$\sqf{3 - 5} = 4$$
For absolute error loss:
$$\abs{3 - 5} = 2$$

2. For $c = 1$:
The risk under squared error loss is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{\sqf{Y - 1}}
&= 0.5 \cd \sqf{0 - 1} + 0.5 \cd \sqf{4 - 1} \\
&= 0.5 \cd 1 + 0.5 \cd 9 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
$$
The risk under absolute error loss is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{\abs{Y - 1}}
&= 0.5 \cd \abs{0 - 1} + 0.5 \cd \abs{4 - 1} \\
&= 0.5 \cd 1 + 0.5 \cd 3 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

3. For $c = 2$:
The risk under squared error loss is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{\sqf{Y - 2}}
&= 0.5 \cd \sqf{0 - 2} + 0.5 \cd \sqf{4 - 2} \\
&= 0.5 \cd 4 + 0.5 \cd 4 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
$$
The risk under absolute error loss is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{\abs{Y - 2}}
&= 0.5 \cd \abs{0 - 2} + 0.5 \cd \abs{4 - 2} \\
&= 0.5 \cd 2 + 0.5 \cd 2 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

4. The prediction $c = 2$ has the smaller risk under squared error loss ($4$ versus $5$).
The two predictions have the same risk under absolute error loss ($2$),
so under absolute error loss this exercise does not choose one of them.
The prediction $c = 2$ equals the expectation:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{Y}
&= 0.5 \cd 0 + 0.5 \cd 4 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
